Photograph: Andrii Marienko/AP Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Russia attacks multiple power plants after Trump energy ceasefire claim Zelenskyy says Ukrainian skies filled with Russian drones after truce claim, which Moscow has yet to confirm, as six killed in strikes. What we know on day 1,692 Guardian staff and agencies Sun 11 Oct 2026 22.05 EDT Last modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 23.20 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Russian strikes hit multiple Ukrainian power plants after Donald Trump claimed both sides had agreed to stop hitting each other’s energy infrastructure, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said . The Ukrainian president said on social media a drone had hit a power plant in Kyiv on Sunday, leading to power outages in the capital. Shortly after, he said there had been a strike on the CHP-5 power plant in the eastern city of Kharkiv, adding:“Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian ‘shaheds’ [drones] all day.” Trump said earlier that “effective immediately, there is an energy ceasefire in the war between Russia and Ukraine”. “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” the US president wrote on his Truth Social platform on Sunday morning in Washington, without further details. Zelenskyy expressed surprise at the announcement, saying the deal was “news to me” and he was seeking further details. Russia has yet to confirm it agreed. The ceasefire appeared to garner support on Sunday from Ukraine’s key western allies , including the UK, France, Canada and the European Commission. British prime minister Andy Burnham said a sustained energy ceasefire was “the best route to get energy and fuel back into world markets”. French president Emmanuel Macron said Paris supported a “real energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine. Ukrainian officials said Russian ⁠attacks killed six people ⁠in two Ukrainian ⁠cities ​on Sunday , including a strike ⁠on a grocery store in Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-largest city, ​where ‌three people died ‌and 20 were ‌injured. Two children were ‌among the injured, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said. In a separate ​attack ​in western ​Ukraine, officials ​said ‌a Russian strike ​killed ​three people. Trump’s energy truce claim came two days after he announced a controversial agreement to buy Russian diesel fuel while temporarily easing US sanctions, prompting outrage from Ukraine and its European allies, who said it would embolden Moscow. Canadian prime minister Mark Carney added to the chorus of disapproval after a Sunday call with Zelenskyy, saying the diesel deal “is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe”. EU chief Ursula von der Leyen also backed Zelenskyy “as he leads the fight for his people’s freedom”, while Germany foreign minister Johann Wadephul said Berlin continued to “fully support” him. Trump lashed out at Zelenskyy when asked about criticism of the Russia diesel deal , saying it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president” who would finally settle the war. Zelenskyy pushed back, telling US ABC News on Sunday: “First of all, with all respect to President Trump, it’s up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader.” The Trump administration is threatening to stop the procurement system that provides Ukraine with weapons in order to press Kyiv to halt its deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, the Financial Times quoted officials in Europe as saying. The US was lobbying European capitals and Kyiv in an attempt to end the attacks on Russian oil refineries, they said. A Ukrainian ⁠drone killed one ⁠person in Russia’s ⁠border ​Belgorod region on Sunday , ⁠officials said. The operational headquarters ⁠in Belgorod ​region said the drone struck a car on a road ‌near the border. In the ​part of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region ⁠held by Russian ​forces, Moscow-installed ​officials ​said one ​person ‌had been killed ​in ​a Ukrainian attack. Russia’s military ⁠said it ⁠struck ⁠a logistics ​centre in southern Ukraine’s ⁠Mykolaiv region and a cargo vessel ⁠in the ​Black ‌Sea. The logistics centre in the town ‌of Ternivka was used to ​store military and dual-use cargoes for the ⁠Ukrainian military, the ‌Russian defence ministry ‌claimed on Sunday. The residence, called the Kehlsteinhaus, is above the town of Berchtesgaden. It was one of several buildings in the area used by the Nazi dictator and his entourage during World War Two. Hitler also used the area as a backdrop for propaganda films portraying him as a lover of animals and nature. Local media reported that site had been "largely destroyed", with the public urged to avoid the area. Read more on this story. The left-wing Solidaires union federation said anger over wages, living costs and public services was bringing together students, workers, firefighters and other groups. "We see an aggregation of anger," Solidaires co-leader Murielle Guilbert told broadcaster BFM TV. The SUD Education teaching union said it would join the October 31 demonstrations. The larger CGT union is set to decide during the week. The Yellow Vests movement also called for rallies, including sit-ins outside town halls and the National Assembly. The government has opened talks with unions and student representatives, but protest leaders say its proposals are inadequate. https://p.dw.com/p/5OdwZ Skip next section France reports more than 1,300 arrests after protests 10/25/2026 October 25, 2026 France reports more than 1,300 arrests after protests French authorities detained 1,314 people during nationwide protests on Saturday, according to a provisional Interior Ministry tally. The ministry said 53 police officers and other security personnel were injured, firefighters responded to 75 fires and 24 businesses were looted. It did not provide a figure for injured protesters. Clashes broke out in cities including Paris, Marseille, Bordeaux, Toulouse and Tours, with police using tear gas . The ministry blamed groups including radical far-left activists for confrontations along or near protest routes. Authorities counted 410,000 participants at 289 demonstrations and gatherings, down from 550,000 a week earlier. Other estimates put Saturday's turnout as high as 800,000. The reported arrests and violence were substantially lower than on October 17, when authorities recorded 2,628 detentions and 1,144 injured security personnel. The number is expected to rise as security officials tally up the day's events, Nunez added. "Multiple lootings have been averted," he said. While some clashes between protesters and police were reported in many French cities, the scope of the unrest was much smaller compared to the protests last Saturday , which saw buildings defaced and burned, and some 1,500 shops looted across the country. Business owners told me they were worried more looting might lie ahead, after gangs of individuals had ransacked and destroyed at least 3,000 shops across the country last weekend. "Some of us are planning to buy weapons to defend ourselves, in case the pillagers come back. One day, there's going to be a tragedy — for sure," Jonathan Siad, owner of a tobacco shop in Paris, said to me. Other store owners were too afraid to talk to us in front of the camera – they worried criminals might see the interview and target their shop. Residents told me they would try to avoid the area where the demonstration was taking place. Only to add that they hoped the situation wouldn't escalate like last week, when even places far away from the actual marches became hotspots of clashes between the police and protesters. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez had admitted on Monday a "loss of control" last Saturday. The authorities thus increased the number of police deployed across France by 10,000 to 70,000 this Saturday. First clashes between protesters and the police started to occur in the late afternoon in several cities across France such as Marseille, Lyon and Paris. But for now, the much feared mass looting and ransacking doesn't seem to be happening. The situation is nowhere near the total chaos Paris and other cities like Marseille experienced last Saturday. "Last weekend, our neighborhood resembled a war zone with gangs roaming the area. Today, it's completely empty apart from police with their vans," Yassaman Metghalchi, co-owner of a jewelry shop in the city center of Paris that got looted last Saturday, told me.
